title: Division with remainders and long division
summary: Write a division digit by digit, see what a {{term:remainder}} is and what to do with it in a problem, and check a division by multiplying.
guide: Sometimes things share out equally with nothing left over. Sometimes a few are left over: that is the {{term:remainder}}. Put 17 flowers equally into 4 vases and each vase gets 4 flowers, with 1 flower left over.

In the written method (the bus stop), the {{term:divisor}} sits outside the bracket on the left and the {{term:dividend}} goes inside. You write the {{term:quotient}} on top, above the digits, and the subtractions underneath.

Each step has three jobs: find how many times the {{term:divisor}} goes into the number and write that digit on top; multiply that digit by the {{term:divisor}} and write the answer underneath; then subtract. If there is another digit, bring it down and do the same again.
The {{term:remainder}} is always smaller than the {{term:divisor}}. If it is bigger or the same, the {{term:divisor}} still goes in at least once more.
To {{term:check}} a division, multiply the {{term:quotient}} by the {{term:divisor}} and add the {{term:remainder}}. You should get the {{term:dividend}} back.
Every right digit turns green. If you get stuck, press “Show me this step”.

engine.label-wrong: Not yet! Work this digit out again.

flowers.title: 17 flowers in 4 vases
flowers.prompt: Sara has 17 flowers to put equally into 4 vases. Divide 17 by 4 and fill in the boxes.
flowers.hint: How many 4s go into 17? 4 × 4 = 16 and 5 × 4 = 20. 20 is more than 17, so it is 4.
flowers.success: Well done! Each vase gets 4 flowers and 1 flower is left over.
flowers.why: Why isn't the {{term:quotient}} 5? Could the {{term:remainder}} be 4 or more?
flowers.model: For 5 flowers in every vase you would need 5 × 4 = 20 flowers, but Sara only has 17. The {{term:remainder}} can't be 4 or more either: if 4 flowers were left, each vase could get one more. So the {{term:remainder}} is always smaller than the {{term:divisor}}.

feedback.wrong: Some boxes are still empty. Fill them in one by one; the question under the division helps you.

cars.title: How many cars?
cars.prompt: 30 children are going on a trip. Each car takes 4 children. First divide 30 by 4. Then type the smallest number of cars that can take everyone.
cars.hint: 30 ÷ 4 is 7 remainder 2. Those 2 children need to come on the trip too!
cars.success: Right! 7 cars are full and 2 children are left, so they need one more car: 8 cars.
cars.why: The {{term:quotient}} is 7. So why is the answer 8 cars?
cars.model: 7 cars only take 7 × 4 = 28 children, so 2 children would be left behind. They need another car, even though it won't be full. That makes 7 + 1 = 8 cars. In a problem you have to think about what the {{term:remainder}} means.

feedback.dropped-remainder: 7 cars take 7 × 4 = 28 children. What about the other 2?
feedback.gave-remainder: 2 is the {{term:remainder}}: the children left without a seat. We want the number of cars.
feedback.wrote-both: You wrote 7 and 2 next to each other: 7 full cars and 2 children left. Now type just how many cars you need.
feedback.too-big: Too many: with that many cars, some would be empty.
feedback.too-small: Too few: with that many cars, some children would be left behind.
feedback.empty: Type the number of cars in the box.

three-digits.prompt: 745 books are packed equally into 3 boxes. Divide 745 by 3.
three-digits.hint: First share out just the 7 hundreds between 3. Then read the remainder together with the 4: 14 tens.
three-digits.success: Well done! Each box gets 248 books, with 1 book left over.
three-digits.why: In the second step, why did we divide 14 and not 4?
three-digits.model: In the first step 6 hundreds were shared out and 1 hundred was left. 1 hundred is 10 tens. Together with the 4 tens we already had, that makes 14 tens. That is why the 4 was brought down next to the 1.

feedback.wrong: Some boxes are still empty. Remember to bring down the next digit after each subtraction.

two-digit-divisor.title: Dividing by a 2-digit number
two-digit-divisor.prompt: Reza puts 296 pencils into packs of 12. Divide 296 by 12.
two-digit-divisor.hint: 12 doesn't go into 2, so look at 29. 2 × 12 = 24 and 3 × 12 = 36. Which one is not more than 29?
two-digit-divisor.success: Excellent! That makes 24 packs, with 8 pencils left over.
two-digit-divisor.why: When you got to 56, how did you know the next digit of the {{term:quotient}} was 4?
two-digit-divisor.model: I tried multiples of 12: 4 × 12 = 48 is not more than 56, but 5 × 12 = 60 is too much. So it is 4. The {{term:remainder}} is 56 − 48 = 8, which is smaller than 12.

feedback.wrong: Some boxes are still empty. If you get stuck, list the multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60.

check-it.title: Check the answer
check-it.prompt: Maryam divided 95 by 4. Her working is above: {{term:quotient}} 23, {{term:remainder}} 3. To {{term:check}} it, work out 23 × 4 + 3.
check-it.hint: First work out 23 × 4. Then add the {{term:remainder}}.
check-it.success: Well done! 23 × 4 + 3 = 95. You got back to the {{term:dividend}}, so Maryam's division is right.
check-it.why: Why does {{term:quotient}} × {{term:divisor}} + {{term:remainder}} give back the {{term:dividend}} when the division is right?
check-it.model: 95 nuts were shared between 4 people: each got 23 and 3 were left. Putting them all back together gives 4 lots of 23 (23 × 4 = 92) plus the 3 left over: 92 + 3 = 95. Multiplying undoes dividing.

feedback.forgot-remainder: 23 × 4 = 92 is right, but don't forget the {{term:remainder}}: add the 3.
feedback.took-remainder: You took the {{term:remainder}} away. Those 3 were part of the 95 too: add them.
feedback.added-divisor: Here you need to multiply 23 by 4, not add 4.
feedback.too-big: Too big. Work out 23 × 4 again first.
feedback.too-small: Too small. Work out 23 × 4 again, then add the 3.
feedback.empty: Type your answer in the box.
